title: Embracing the Buddha's Dhamma: The 1956 Revolution
summary: Fulfilling his 1935 vow—'I was born a Hindu, but I shall not die a Hindu'—Ambedkar chose Buddhism as the only world path founded on empirical reason, compassion, and absolute human equality.
keywords: Embracing the Buddha's Dhamma: The 1956 Revolution
full_text:
In 1935, at the Yeola conference in Maharashtra, Dr. Ambedkar made a solemn declaration:
"I was born an untouchable Hindu. That was beyond my power. But I solemnly assure you: **I will not die a Hindu!**"

That vow reverberated across the globe. Powerful religious delegations from Islam and Christianity courted Ambedkar:
"Join our faith with your followers, Dr. Ambedkar! We will provide limitless funds and global political leverage!"

Ambedkar rejected them outright:
"I am not in the business of auctioning the souls of my people! Changing faith is not a matter of swapping cultural labels; it is an existential search for liberty, equality, and compassion."

For twenty-one years, Ambedkar conducted an exhaustive comparative study of world religions. His intellectual quest led him to the Dhamma of Gautama Buddha.

On October 14, 1956, at Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, history unfolded.

Over five hundred thousand men, women, and children gathered, draped in pristine white garments. It was the largest voluntary religious conversion in human history.

Taking the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts from Venerable U Chandramani, Ambedkar embraced Buddhism, and subsequently administered the 22 vows to the vast multitude.

Addressing the congregation, Ambedkar explained:
"Comrades! Why did I choose the Buddha?
Other religions dwell on supernatural deities, invisible souls, and eternal hells to manipulate human fear.
The Buddha alone declared: 'Do not believe anything merely on my authority; examine my teachings with your own reason, and embrace them only if they lead to the welfare of all!'
In the Buddha's Dhamma, there is no caste, no untouchability, and no subjection of women.
Compassion (*Karuna*) and Wisdom (*Prajna*) are its twin pillars!

Today, we are reborn. We are no longer untouchables; we are free, autonomous citizens walking in the radiant light of reason!"

His radiant smile reflected the culmination of a lifelong crusade for inner and outer emancipation.
moral: Faith must liberate the human intellect and affirm equality; moral autonomy is the pinnacle of spiritual maturity.
